title: Two Sum
statement:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the **indices** of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the answer with the smaller index first.
hints: Brute force works: check every pair. But can you do it in one pass?
As you scan the array, ask: "have I already seen the number that would complete this pair?" What data structure answers that in O(1)?
Keep a Map from value → index. For each nums[i], look up target - nums[i] in the map before inserting nums[i].

title: Valid Parentheses
statement:
Given a string `s` containing just the characters `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[` and `]`, determine if the input string is **valid**.

A string is valid if:
1. Open brackets are closed by the same type of bracket.
2. Open brackets are closed in the correct order.
3. Every close bracket has a corresponding open bracket.
hints: Think about the *most recently opened* bracket — it has to be closed first. What data structure is 'last in, first out'?
Push opening brackets onto a stack. When you hit a closing bracket, what should be on top of the stack?
Pop on every closer and compare types; the string is valid only if every pop matches and the stack ends empty.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum, and return **its sum**.
hints: For each position, there are only two choices: extend the previous subarray, or start fresh here. When is starting fresh better?
Track a running sum. If it ever drops below zero, it can only hurt whatever comes next — reset it.
This is Kadane's algorithm: current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]); best = max(best, current). Watch out for all-negative arrays.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string `s`, find the length of the **longest substring** without duplicate characters.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces
hints: A substring is a *window* into the string. Can you grow a window on the right and shrink it on the left only when needed?
Keep a Set (or Map of char → last index) of what's inside the window. When you hit a duplicate, move the left edge forward.

Sliding window: advance right pointer each step; while s[right] is in the window, remove s[left] and advance left. Track max window size. The 'abba' case is why a Map of last-seen indices needs a max() when jumping left.

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input, sorted by start.
hints: Overlaps are much easier to spot when the intervals are in a helpful order. What should you sort by?
After sorting by start, two adjacent intervals overlap exactly when the next one's start <= the current merged end.
Sort by start, keep a 'current' interval, and either extend its end (end = max(end, next.end)) or push it and start a new one.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is the product of all elements of `nums` **except** `nums[i]`.

You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and **without using division**.
hints: The product excluding position i is (everything to the left of i) × (everything to the right of i).
Can you build an array of prefix products in one pass, and suffix products in another?
Two passes: first fill answer[i] with the product of everything left of i; then sweep right-to-left multiplying in a running suffix product.

title: Coin Change
statement:
You are given an integer array `coins` representing coin denominations and an integer `amount`.

Return the **fewest number of coins** needed to make up `amount`. If it cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`. You may assume an infinite supply of each coin.
hints: Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails — try coins [1,3,4] with amount 6. What technique handles 'best way to build up to X'?
Define dp[a] = fewest coins to make amount a. How does dp[a] relate to dp[a - coin] for each coin?
Bottom-up DP: dp[0]=0, dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over all coins c <= a. Use Infinity for unreachable amounts and return -1 if dp[amount] is still Infinity.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute **how much water** it can trap after raining.
hints: Focus on a single column: how much water sits *on top of it*? It depends on the tallest wall to its left and the tallest to its right.
water[i] = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) - height[i], clamped at 0. Can you precompute maxLeft and maxRight arrays?
Two-pointer refinement: move the pointer on the side with the smaller max; that side's water is decided by its own max alone.
